name: GDP per capita, PPP
definition: Gross domestic product divided by midyear population, converted using purchasing power parity rates and expressed in constant 2021 international dollars.
interpretation: Higher values indicate greater average economic output per person after adjusting for price differences between countries.
whyItMatters: It is a useful measure of average material resources, but it does not show how income is distributed or whether growth is sustainable.
caveat: GDP per capita is not household income, does not measure unpaid work or wellbeing, and can be distorted by multinational activity or resource rents.

name: GDP per capita growth
definition: Annual percentage growth in real GDP per capita.
interpretation: Positive values mean average real economic output per person increased during the year; negative values mean it fell.
whyItMatters: It distinguishes economic expansion that outpaces population growth from growth driven mainly by a larger population.
caveat: One-year growth is volatile. Interpret it alongside five-year trends, distribution, and starting income levels.

name: Gross domestic product
definition: The market value of final goods and services produced within a country during the year, converted to current US dollars.
interpretation: This measures the overall size of an economy. It should be read alongside population, GDP per capita, real growth, and price-level measures.
whyItMatters: Economic scale affects fiscal capacity, market size, geopolitical weight, and the resources potentially available to society.
caveat: Current-dollar GDP is affected by inflation and exchange rates, does not measure distribution or wellbeing, and is not suitable by itself for comparing living standards.

name: Inflation, consumer prices
definition: Annual percentage change in the cost to the average consumer of acquiring a basket of goods and services.
interpretation: Very high or unstable inflation erodes purchasing power, while deflation can also signal economic weakness.
whyItMatters: Price stability shapes household purchasing power, planning, savings, and the real value of wages and public budgets.
caveat: Consumer baskets and data quality differ between countries, and national averages can hide different experiences across households.

name: Gini index
definition: The Gini index measures how far the distribution of income or consumption differs from perfect equality, where 0 is perfect equality and 100 is perfect inequality.
interpretation: A lower score indicates a more equal measured distribution. The score does not identify where in the distribution inequality occurs.
whyItMatters: National averages can conceal large differences in living standards and access to opportunity.
caveat: Some countries measure income and others consumption. Survey years, coverage, and methods differ, so exact comparisons require care.

name: Life expectancy at birth
definition: The number of years a newborn would live if prevailing age-specific mortality patterns stayed constant throughout their life.
interpretation: Higher values usually reflect better survival conditions across the life course.
whyItMatters: It summarizes mortality across all ages and reflects health care, living conditions, safety, and social determinants.
caveat: It is a period estimate, not a prediction for an individual child, and does not describe health quality or inequality within a country.

name: Under-five mortality rate
definition: The probability per 1,000 that a newborn dies before reaching age five, if subject to current age-specific mortality rates.
interpretation: Lower values indicate better child survival conditions.
whyItMatters: Child survival is sensitive to nutrition, sanitation, maternal health, vaccination, primary care, poverty, and conflict.
caveat: Many country values are modelled estimates because complete vital-registration systems are not universally available.

name: Individuals using the Internet
definition: The percentage of individuals who used the Internet from any location during the preceding three months.
interpretation: Higher values indicate broader digital participation, though they do not measure connection quality or affordability.
whyItMatters: Digital access increasingly affects education, work, public services, information, and political participation.
caveat: Survey methods and estimation practices differ, and national averages can conceal gender, income, age, and rural–urban gaps.

name: Infant mortality rate
definition: The probability per 1,000 that a newborn dies before reaching one year of age, if subject to current age-specific mortality rates.
interpretation: Lower values indicate better infant survival conditions.
whyItMatters: Infant survival is highly sensitive to maternal care, nutrition, sanitation, vaccination, household conditions, and access to primary health services.
caveat: Many values are modelled by the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation because complete vital-registration data are not available everywhere.

name: Access to electricity
definition: The percentage of the population with access to electricity.
interpretation: Higher values indicate wider access to a foundational service.
whyItMatters: Reliable electricity enables health care, education, communication, household safety, and productive economic activity.
caveat: The measure records access, not reliability, affordability, hours of supply, or the carbon intensity of generation.

name: PM2.5 air pollution exposure
definition: Population-weighted average exposure to ambient fine particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter below 2.5 micrometres.
interpretation: Lower concentrations generally mean cleaner ambient air and lower exposure to a major health risk.
whyItMatters: Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs and are associated with cardiovascular and respiratory harm.
caveat: National averages can hide severe urban or local hotspots and combine monitoring with modelled estimates.

name: Tax revenue
definition: Compulsory, unrequited payments to government, expressed as a share of gross domestic product.
interpretation: The value indicates the scale of tax resources relative to the economy, not whether taxation is equitable or spending effective.
whyItMatters: Revenue capacity affects the ability of governments to finance services, infrastructure, redistribution, and resilience.
caveat: Coverage can differ by level of government, and resource revenues or social contributions may sit outside this measure.

name: Voice and accountability
definition: A composite score of perceptions of citizens’ ability to participate in selecting government, freedom of expression, freedom of association, and free media.
interpretation: Higher values indicate stronger perceived voice and accountability relative to the WGI’s fixed reference points.
whyItMatters: Participation, civic freedoms, and independent information are central to public accountability and provide an important—though incomplete—lens on democratic conditions.
caveat: This is a perception-based composite, not a complete democracy index. WGI scores have uncertainty, can obscure institutional detail, and were recalculated back to 1996 under the 2025 methodology revision.

name: Government effectiveness
definition: A composite score of perceptions of public-service quality, civil-service quality and independence, policy formulation and implementation, and government commitment to its policies.
interpretation: Higher values indicate stronger perceived government effectiveness relative to the WGI’s fixed reference points.
whyItMatters: State capability affects whether laws, budgets, and policy commitments translate into reliable services and real outcomes.
caveat: This broad perception-based composite cannot diagnose which agency or reform is responsible. WGI scores have uncertainty and were recalculated under the 2025 methodology revision.

name: Rule of law
definition: A composite score of perceptions of confidence in and adherence to society’s rules, including contract enforcement, property rights, police, courts, crime, and violence.
interpretation: Higher values indicate stronger perceived rule-of-law conditions relative to the WGI’s fixed reference points.
whyItMatters: Predictable and fairly applied rules shape personal security, rights protection, public trust, and economic coordination.
caveat: This is a broad perception-based composite with uncertainty; it does not measure equal treatment for every group or identify specific justice-system failures.

name: Control of corruption
definition: A composite score of perceptions of the extent to which public power is exercised for private gain, including petty and grand corruption and state capture.
interpretation: Higher values indicate stronger perceived control of corruption relative to the WGI’s fixed reference points; it is not the amount of corruption observed directly.
whyItMatters: Corruption can divert resources, weaken service delivery, distort policy, undermine equal treatment, and reduce institutional trust.
caveat: The score combines perception-based sources and has uncertainty. It should be triangulated with audits, enforcement data, procurement evidence, and lived-experience surveys.
